records.expected: We audited arXiv:1910.10819 version 2 claim by claim. Of 23 verdicts, 8 checked out, 4 were errors, 6 were unsupported, 3 were fitted after the observations, 1 was unfalsifiable as stated, and 1 lay outside this audit. The surviving physical core is narrow: if the universe has a preferred spin axis, clockwise and counterclockwise galaxy counts might differ. The paper supplies no trustworthy size for that difference.

records.expected: The paper identifies cosmic spin with observed dark energy. Follow that statement forward, and dark energy requires rotation at 0.828 times the cosmic expansion rate: 1.09 billion times above the generous Planck rotation bound, and 17.6 billion times above the tighter Saadeh bound. Follow it backward instead, enforcing the generous bound, and rotation supplies less than 1 billion-billionth of observed dark energy. The text provides no third reading.

records.expected: A second failure is independent of the first. The paper says the universe conserves angular momentum as it expands. That premise makes the spin fade with the square of cosmic growth, so its proposed rotational energy thins exactly like radiation. On the paper's own terms, the result cannot accelerate the universe. It also lies about 46 standard deviations from the dark-energy measurement the paper cites as support. The claims fail; the author is not the target.

records.expected: The spin-fade law was derived from a pinned vector-perturbation equation and checked by machine algebra. During radiation domination, rotation falls in inverse proportion to cosmic size. During matter and dark-energy domination, it falls with the inverse square. The inflation-era rate has no pinned source, so it remains an explicit parameter rather than a claimed result. Mapping today's microwave-background limit back to galaxy spin-up changes the allowance by only a factor of a few, not enough to rescue it.

records.expected: Next came the missing bridge: how much galaxy handedness appears per unit of leftover cosmic spin. Combining tidal-torque growth, turnaround, halo spin statistics, and a coherent rotational push gives a transfer coefficient of about 7.2, with an honest bracket from 1.4 to 12.8. Machine algebra reproduced the coefficient and its bounds. Our local novelty check found no printed analytic transfer function of this kind. The strict model still awaits external theorist review before any publication claim.

Favorable choices across the full bracket reach at most 0.08 standard deviations. No survey lever closes that gap.

records.expected: The earlier generous estimate needed 18 observable universes. The derived model needs about 12,000, landing inside the old declared bracket but 25 times below its generous edge. The same chain also turns the microwave-background limit around: inherited parent spin must be diluted by more than 10 to the power 22 for a supermassive parent, or 10 to the power 30 for a stellar parent. That constraint is real but weak: it rules out too little dilution, not parent spin itself.

We tested 1 rotating-parent paper, preserved its bare symmetry idea, froze the strongest explicit model we could justify, derived the missing transfer, and pushed every uncertain lever in its favor. The result is stronger than the earlier generous closure. The idea's best version now exists on the record with its own number, and the number says the route stays closed.
